Consider a system of linear equations and its respective augmented matrix $M\mathbin{:}$


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+z &=6 \\ y-3z &=-13 \\ -x-y-z &=-4\end{aligned}\right. \qquad M = \left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & -4\end{array} \right]
$$



We can reduce $M$ to row echelon form using the standard Gaussian elimination algorithm. The algorithm that we use is very similar to the case of $2 \times 2$ systems. 

Our goal is to create a descending "staircase" of $1$'s with $0$'s below, and we achieve this using elementary row operations. So, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ -1 & -1 & -1 & -4\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & -2 & 0 & 2\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & 0 & -6 & -24\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{6}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ 0 & 1 & -3 & -13 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The matrix is now in row echelon form, and we can apply back substitution to solve the original system of equations.

**Note:** The row echelon form of a matrix is *not* unique.  In the previous example, after the second row operation we arrived at



$$
\left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}{\color{red}1} & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & -3 & -13 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}-6} & -24\end{array}\right].
$$



This augmented matrix is already in row echelon form! However, it is always useful to do an extra step and obtain $1$'s along the main diagonal, like we did previously:



$$
\left[ \begin{array}{ccc|c}{\color{red}1} & -1 & 1 & 6 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & -3 & -13 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & 4\end{array}\right]
$$



Having $1$'s along the main diagonal makes the final back substitution process a little easier.

The **standard Gaussian elimination** for a $3 \times 3$ system can be described as follows:

1. If $a_{11} \neq 0$ and $a_{11} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_1:=R_1/a_{11}.$

2. We use first row and the necessary row operations to make the remaining entries of the first column below $a_{11}$ equal to $0.$ Namely,

   - if $a_{21} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_2:=R_2 + (-a_{21})R_1;$
   - if $a_{31} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{31})R_1.$

3. If $a_{22} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_2:=R_2/a_{22}.$

4. We use the second row and the necessary row operation to make the entry below $a_{22}$ equal to $0.$ Namely,

   - if $a_{32} \neq 0,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3 + (-a_{32})R_2.$

5. If $a_{33} \neq 1,$ then we use the row operation $R_3:=R_3/a_{33}.$

6. In some exceptional cases, such as when the element on the diagonal is equal to $0,$ we first need to exchange rows. Then proceed using the same steps as above.

Carrying out the above algorithm will convert the matrix to row echelon form.

Remember that the **identity matrix** $I_n$ is an $n \times n$ square matrix with $1$'s on the diagonal, and where all other elements are $0.$ For example, the $3 \times 3$ identity matrix $I_3$ is given below: $$ I_3 = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} $$ The identity matrix gets its name from the fact that whenever we multiply a matrix by the corresponding identity matrix, the matrix remains unchanged. For example, let's consider the matrix
$A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 & 10 \\ 6 & -2 & 2 \\ 23 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}$
Multiplying the matrix $A$ by the identity matrix $I_3,$ we find that the result is just $A$ itself: $$ \begin{aligned}A\cdot {I}_{3} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 & 10 \\ 6 & -2 & 2 \\ 23 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}(-2)\cdot 1+3\cdot 0+10\cdot 0 & (-2)\cdot 0+3\cdot 1+10\cdot 0 & (-2)\cdot 0+3\cdot 0+10\cdot 1 \\ 6\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot 0+2\cdot 0 & 6\cdot 0+(-2)\cdot 1+2\cdot 0 & 6\cdot 0+(-2)\cdot 0+2\cdot 1 \\ 23\cdot 1+4\cdot 0+8\cdot 0 & 23\cdot 0+4\cdot 1+8\cdot 0 & 23\cdot 0+4\cdot 0+8\cdot 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 & 10 \\ 6 & -2 & 2 \\ 23 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} \\ & =A\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $A \cdot I_3 = A.$ You can check that $I_3 \cdot A = A$ using the same method. This result holds in general: > For *any* square $n \times n$ matrix $A,$ we have > > > $$ > A \cdot I_n = I_n \cdot A = A. > $$ In other words, the $n \times n$ identity matrix $I_n$ has a similar property to the number $1,$ namely that $$ a\cdot 1 = 1\cdot a = a $$ for any real number $a.$

Whenever we multiply a matrix $A$ by the $n$th column of the identity matrix, the result is the $n$th column of $A.$ For example, consider the matrix
$A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$
The first column of the identity matrix $I_2$ is given by $$ \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} $$ If we multiply $A$ by the column on the *right*, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}{\color{blue}{3}} & -1 \\ {\color{blue}{1}} & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 1\cdot 1+2\cdot 0\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}{\color{blue}{3}} \\ {\color{blue}{1}}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ The product is just the first column of the matrix $A.$ Using the same method, you can check for yourself that when we multiply $A$ by the second column of $I_2,$ the result is the second column of $A.$ On the other hand, if we multiply $A$ by the first *row* of the identity matrix $I_2$ on the *left*, we will obtain the first row of $A$. Indeed, $$ \begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{\color{blue}{3}} & {\color{blue}{-1}} \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3\cdot 1+1\cdot 0 & (-1)\cdot 1+2\cdot 0\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}{\color{blue}{3}} & {\color{blue}{-1}}\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$

We've been using the fact that $AI_n = I_n A = A$ for any $n \times n$ matrix $A.$ But how do we know for sure?

Let's prove the case of $n=2.$ That is, let's prove that $AI_2=I_2A = A,$ where $A$ is any $2\times2$ matrix.

Any general $2 \times 2$ matrix can be written as
$$
A =
	\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix}.
$$ 

Then, multiplying by $I_2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A{I}_{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11}\cdot 1+{a}_{12}\cdot 0 & {a}_{11}\cdot 0+{a}_{12}\cdot 1 \\ {a}_{21}\cdot 1+{a}_{22}\cdot 0 & {a}_{21}\cdot 0+{a}_{22}\cdot 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =A.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2}A & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =A.\end{aligned}
$$

The above proof shows that the property $A I_2 = I_2 A = A$ holds for all $2\times2$ matrices $A.$

In general, to prove that the property $AI_n = I_n A = A$ holds for all $n \times n$ matrices $A,$ we can use the same method.

Let's consider a system of linear equations where the corresponding coefficient matrix is singular. For example, consider the following system and its associated augmented matrix:


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y &=-5 \\ -3x+6y &=15\end{aligned}\right. \qquad M = \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -2 & -5 \\ -3 & 6 & 15\end{array} \right]
$$



To solve the system, we can reduce $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as usual. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -2 & -5 \\ -3 & 6 & 15\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -2 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y &=-5 \\ 0x+0y &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$



Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y = 0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x - 2y = -5.
$$

Finally, we describe the **general solution** of our system.

- The first variable in our equation, $x,$ is called a **basic variable**.

- The second variable in our equation, $y,$ is called a **free variable**.

Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x = -5+2y.$ So the general solution of the system is


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=-5+2y \\ y &=y\end{aligned}\right.
$$


where the free variable $y$ is any number.

In vector form, this solution is written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-5+2y \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-5 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+y\begin{bmatrix}2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix},\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this is the equation of a straight line on a plane. Any point on this line satisfies our system of equations.

If we want to find some **particular solution** of the system, we simply choose some particular value of $y$ and find the corresponding value of $x$ on the line. For example, if we choose $y=0,$ then the corresponding value is $x=-5$ and the particular solution is $x=-5,$ $y=0.$

Given a $2 \times 2$ system of linear equations, we have the following possibilities for the number of solutions:

- The system has exactly *one solution* if and only if the respective coefficient matrix is non-singular (meaning that the determinant is not zero). Such systems are called **consistent independent**.

- The system has *infinitely many solutions* if the second row in the standard echelon form contains only $0$'s. These systems are called **consistent dependent**.

- The system has *no solution* if the second row in the standard echelon form contains only $0$'s on the left-hand side and a non-zero element on the right-hand side. These are called **inconsistent** systems.

![](images/16/1692fbea298339ff839cf2f14986d51af45d1ec72b2b7d0de179336bdef40c0e.png)

**Note:** A system of linear equations of the form 


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}ax+by &=0 \\ cx+dy &=0,\end{aligned}\right.
$$


where we have only $0$'s on the right-hand side, is called **homogeneous**. A homogeneous system always has at least one solution, namely, the solution $x=0$ and $y=0.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle 0,0 \rangle.$

Sometimes, a system of equations might not have any solutions. For example, consider the following augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}M=\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 10\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y &=3 \\ 0x+0y &=10.\end{aligned}\right.
$$



The final equation, $0x+0y=10,$ has no solution. It simplifies to $0=10,$ which is a false statement.

So, there is no pair $x,y$ that satisfies both equations in the system. Consequently, the overall system has no solution.

Just like for $2\times 2$ matrices, there are also **elementary $3\times 3$ matrices**. These are matrices that can be obtained by applying *only one* elementary row operation to the identity matrix $I_3 ={\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array} \right]}.$

For instance, consider the following $3\times 3$ matrices:

$$
E_1 = {\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array} \right]}, \quad
E_2 = {\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array} \right]}, \quad
E_3 = {\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array} \right]}.
$$

These are all examples of elementary matrices:

- $E_1$ is obtained from $I_3$ by applying the row operation $R_1 \leftrightarrow R_2.$

- $E_2$ is obtained from $I_3$ by applying the row operation $R_2 := 2R_2.$

- $E_3$ is obtained from $I_3$ by applying the row operation $R_2 := R_2 + 3R_1.$

They are also examples of the three different types of elementary matrices, defined by the corresponding row operations.

As we saw before for elementary $2\times 2$ matrices, each elementary $3\times 3$ matrix $E$ is invertible, and the corresponding inverse is always an elementary matrix of the same type as $E.$ To illustrate, let's consider the matrix 

$$
E = {\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array} \right]}.
$$

To find the inverse of $E,$ we proceed as follows:

**Step 1:** Write down $\color{blue}E$ and the identity matrix $I_3$ side-by-side, as shown below:
$$
[{\color{blue}{E}}\, |\, {\color{black}I_3}]	
=	
\left[{\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}{\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}4} & {\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}0} & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}1} & 0 & 0 & 1\end{array}}\right]
$$

**Step 2:** Apply an elementary row operation that transforms the left matrix into the identity matrix. In our case, we need to apply the transformation $R_2 := R_2 + (-4)R_1.$ We apply the operation to entire row (not only the left part):

$$
\begin{aligned}[E\,|\,{I}_{3}] & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 4 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} &  & {R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|ccc}1 & 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & -4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 & 1\end{array}\right] \\  & =[{I}_{3}\,|\,{E}^{-1}]\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $R_2 := R_2 + (-4)R_1$ transforms $E$ back into the identity matrix. Likewise, when this row operation is applied to the identity matrix, it generates $E^{-1}.$

The matrix $E^{-1}$ is obtained on the right-hand side of our big matrix after the transformation. Therefore,
$$
E^{-1} = 
{\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0 & 0 \\ - 4 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array} \right]}.
$$

We can work out the inverse of all elementary $3\times 3$ matrices in a similar way.

Remember the following three standard elementary row operations: 

  I. Swapping two rows

  II. Multiplying a row by a non-zero number

  III. Adding a multiple of one row to another row

Of these three elementary row operations, only III (adding a multiple of one row to another row) *preserves* the determinant. The other two operations, switching two rows or multiplying a row by a non-zero number, *change* the determinant.

To demonstrate, let's consider the matrix $A = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{array} \right]}.$ Taking the determinant, we have
$$
\left| {\begin{array}{cc}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{array}} \right| = 1 \cdot 4 - 2 \cdot 3 = -2.
$$

If we swap the two rows, we get a different determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} & =3\cdot 2-1\cdot 4 \\  & =2 \\  & \ne -2\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Likewise, if we multiply top row by ${\color{red}2},$ then we get a different determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}2\cdot 1 & 2\cdot 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} & =\begin{vmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =2\cdot 4-3\cdot 4 \\  & =-4 \\  & \ne -2\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

However, if we add twice the top row to the bottom row, then we get the same determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3+2\cdot 1 & 4+2\cdot 2\end{vmatrix} & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 5 & 8\end{vmatrix} \\  & =1\cdot 8-2\cdot 5 \\  & =-2\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\det(A^T)=\det(A),$ the corresponding elementary column operations on determinants have the same properties as the elementary row ones.

- Swapping two columns changes the sign of the determinant.

- Multiplying a column by a number scales the determinant by that number.

- Adding a multiple of one column to another column does not change the determinant.

Consider a vector $\mathbf{u}$ which is given in terms of the vectors $\mathbf{v_1}$ and $\mathbf{v_2}$ as follows:

$$
{\color{red}3}{\color{blue}\mathbf{v_1}}+({\color{red}-2}){\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}} = \mathbf{u}
$$

Here, we say that $\mathbf{u}$ is a **linear combination** of the vectors ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v_1}}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{v_2}}$ with coefficients ${\color{red}3}$ and ${\color{red}-2}$ respectively. 

In general, a linear combination of $n$ vectors $\mathbf{v_1},\mathbf{v_2},\dots,\mathbf{v_n}$ is the *weighted sum*

$$
{\color{red}x_1}\mathbf{\color{blue}v_1}+{\color{red}x_2}\mathbf{\color{blue}v_2}+\cdots + {\color{red}x_n}\mathbf{\color{blue}v_n} = \mathbf{u},
$$

where ${\color{red}x_1},{\color{red}x_2},\dots,{\color{red}x_n}\in\mathbb{R}.$ We say that $\mathbf{u}$ is a linear combination of the vectors $\mathbf{\color{blue}v_1},\mathbf{\color{blue}v_2},\dots,\mathbf{\color{blue}v_n}$ with coefficients (or *weights*) ${\color{red}x_1},{\color{red}x_2},\dots,{\color{red}x_n},$ respectively.

For instance, 


$$
{\color{red}2} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}}_{\large\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_1} + {\color{red}0} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}\sqrt{2} \\ 3\end{bmatrix}}_{\large\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_2} + {\color{red}\dfrac{1}{2}} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}8 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}}_{\large\color{blue}\mathbf{v}_3}
$$


is the linear combination of vectors $\mathbf{\color{blue}v_1},\mathbf{\color{blue}v_2},\mathbf{\color{blue}v_3}$ with coefficients ${\color{red}2}, {\color{red}0}, {\color{red}\dfrac{1}{2}},$ respectively.

A **basis** of a subspace $U$ (in $\mathbb{R}^n$) is a set of vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ that is linearly independent and spans $U.$

For example, consider the following subspace consisting of the span of three vectors:
$$
U = \textrm{Span}
	\Bigg\{ 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{blue}1} \\ {\color{blue}0}\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{blue}0} \\ {\color{blue}1}\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{red}- 1} \\ {\color{red}3}\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} 
	\Bigg\}
$$

To find a basis of $U,$ we need to find a set of linearly independent vectors that spans $U.$

**Watch out!** The set
$$
\Bigg\{ 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{blue}1} \\ {\color{blue}0}\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{blue}0} \\ {\color{blue}1}\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{red}- 1} \\ {\color{red}3}\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} 
	\Bigg\}
$$
is *not* a basis of $U.$ It's true that this set *spans* $U,$ but the vectors in this set are *not* linearly independent. In particular, the vector $\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3$ can be written as a linear combination of $\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2$ as follows:

$$
\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{red}- 1} \\ {\color{red}3}\end{array} \right]} }_{\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} = 
	(-1) \cdot \underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{blue}1} \\ {\color{blue}0}\end{array} \right]} }_{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1} + 
	3 \cdot \underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{blue}0} \\ {\color{blue}1}\end{array} \right]} }_{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}
$$

To find a basis of $U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \},$ we can start with $\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \},$ but we need to remove any "redundant" vectors that can be written as a linear combination of other vectors in the set. In this case, we remove ${\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3}$ because it can be written as a linear combination of $\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}.$

We are left with the set

$$
\Bigg\{ 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{blue}1} \\ {\color{blue}0}\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}{\color{blue}0} \\ {\color{blue}1}\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}
	\Bigg\}.
$$

These two vectors are linearly independent (since they are not parallel), and removing a redundant vector does not change the span, so these vectors still span $U.$ That is to say,

$$
U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \} = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}.
$$

Therefore, the set $\mathcal{B} = \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}$ is a basis of $U.$

**Note:** To see that the vectors $\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}$ still span $U,$ first note that any vector $\mathbf{b} \in U$ can be written as a linear combination of the three original vectors:

$$
\mathbf{b} = x_1 {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1} + x_2 {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} + x_3 {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3}
$$

Since ${\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} = -{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}+3{\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2},$ then we must have 

$$
\begin{aligned}b & ={x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2}+{x}_{3}(-{a}_{1}+3{a}_{2}) \\  & =({x}_{1}-{x}_{3}){a}_{1}+({x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}){a}_{2},\end{aligned}
$$

which shows that $\mathbf{b}$ can actually be written as a linear combination of only two vectors, ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}$ and ${\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}.$

Therefore, we can conclude that the set $\{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2} \}$ spans the subspace $U = \textrm{Span} \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_1}, {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}_2}, {\color{red}\mathbf{a}_3} \}.$

As we saw, swapping two rows does not preserve the determinant. However, the only difference is the sign of the determinant changes. 

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} & =1\cdot 4-2\cdot 3=-2 \\ \begin{vmatrix}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix} & =3\cdot 2-1\cdot 4=2\end{aligned}
$$

So, in the above example, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} & =-\begin{vmatrix}3 & 4 \\ 1 & 2\end{vmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, swapping any two rows of a matrix changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite one. That is to say, 

$$
\begin{aligned}det\begin{bmatrix}⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ ◻ & ◻ & … & ◻ \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ △ & △ & … & △ \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮\end{bmatrix}=-det\begin{bmatrix}⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ △ & △ & … & △ \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ ◻ & ◻ & … & ◻ \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

As we have seen, multiplying a row by a number does not preserve the determinant. However, it does affect the determinant in a predictable way: multiplying a row by a number scales the determinant by that number as well.

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} & =1\cdot 4-2\cdot 3=-2 \\ \begin{vmatrix}2\cdot 1 & 2\cdot 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix}=\begin{vmatrix}2 & 4 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} & =2\cdot 4-3\cdot 4=-4\end{aligned}
$$

So, in the above example, we have
$$
\left| {\begin{array}{cc}{\color{red}2} \cdot  1 & {\color{red}2} \cdot  2 \\ 3 & 4\end{array}} \right| = {\color{red}2} \cdot \left| {\begin{array}{cc}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{array}} \right|.
$$

In general, multiplying a row of a matrix by a number multiplies the determinant by that number. That is to say, we can factor out the common multiplier from the row of the determinant:

$$
\begin{aligned}det\begin{bmatrix}⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ k△ & k△ & … & k△ \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮\end{bmatrix}=k\cdot det\begin{bmatrix}⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮ \\ △ & △ & … & △ \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & … & ⋮\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The dimension of the column space of a matrix $A$ is called the **rank of $A$**. It's usually denoted by $\textrm{rank}(A)$. So, 

$$
\textrm{rank}(A) = \textrm{dim}(\textrm{Col}(A)).
$$

For example, to find the rank of 


$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 6 & 4 & 10\end{bmatrix},
$$


we write $A$ in row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 6 & 4 & 10\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the reduced matrix above, we see that there are $2$ pivot columns, namely, the $1$st and the $2$nd. This implies that the first and the second columns of $A$ form a basis of $\textrm{Col}(A)$ and, therefore, the dimension of $\textrm{Col}(A)$ is equal to $2.$

Let's check what happens if we multiply the entire matrix (not only one row) by a number. For example,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{vmatrix} & =1\cdot 4-2\cdot 3=-2 \\ \begin{vmatrix}3\cdot 1 & 3\cdot 2 \\ 3\cdot 3 & 3\cdot 4\end{vmatrix}=\begin{vmatrix}3 & 6 \\ 9 & 12\end{vmatrix} & =3\cdot 12-6\cdot 9=-18\end{aligned}
$$

So, in the above example, we have

$$
\left| {\begin{array}{cc}{\color{red}3} \cdot  1 & {\color{red}3} \cdot  2 \\ {\color{red}3} \cdot  3 & {\color{red}3} \cdot  4\end{array}} \right| = {\color{red}3}^2 \cdot \left| {\begin{array}{cc}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{array}} \right|.
$$

The above is equivalent to multiplying both rows of the matrix by $3$. Multiplying the first row scales the determinant by $3$, and then multiplying the second row scales it by $3$ once more.

In general, multiplying an entire $n \times n$ matrix by a number multiplies the determinant by that number to the power of $n$. That is to say, we can factor out the common multiplier from the entire matrix, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(k\cdot A) &={k}^{n}\cdot det(A),\end{aligned}
$$

where $A$ is an $n \times n$ matrix.

In the previous example, it was easy to see that one vector was a linear combination of the others. But what can we do when it's not so easy to tell? For example, consider the subspace

$$
U = \textrm{Span}
	\Bigg\{ 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ - 2\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{black}\mathbf{a}_1}, 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 1 \\ 3\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{black}\mathbf{a}_2}, 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 1 \\ 7\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{black}\mathbf{a}_3} 
	\Bigg\}.
$$

To find a subset of linearly independent vectors, we can put the vectors in a matrix and compute the reduced row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3 & 7\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 5\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent (or redundant) vectors that can be removed. Here, the $1$st and $2$nd columns are pivot columns, while the $3$rd column is a non-pivot column.

**But watch out!** We need to pick the pivot columns from the *original matrix*, not from the reduced one.

The $1$st and $2$nd columns from the original matrix are $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2.$ So, a basis of $U$ is $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ that is to say, 

$$
\mathcal{B} = \Bigg\{ 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ - 2\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{black}\mathbf{a}_1}, 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 1 \\ 3\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{black}\mathbf{a}_2} 
	\Bigg\}.
$$

Earlier, we computed a basis of 

$$
U = \textrm{Span}
	\Bigg\{ 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ - 2\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{black}\mathbf{a}_1}, 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 1 \\ 3\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{black}\mathbf{a}_2}, 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 1 \\ 7\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{black}\mathbf{a}_3} 
	\Bigg\}.
$$

The basis that we found was

$$
\mathcal{B} = \Bigg\{ 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ - 2\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{black}\mathbf{a}_1}, 
		\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 1 \\ 3\end{array} \right]}}_{\color{black}\mathbf{a}_2} 
	\Bigg\}.
$$

The vector $\mathbf{a}_3$ was not included in the basis. This means that $\mathbf{a}_3$ can be written as a linear combination of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2.$

Now, what if we want to find the exact linear combination of $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ that yields $\mathbf{a}_3?$ That is to say, we want to find $x_1, x_2 \in \mathbb{R}$ such that 

$$
{\color{black}x_1} \underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ - 2\end{array} \right]}}_{\mathbf{a}_1} + {\color{rblack}x_2} \underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 1 \\ 3\end{array} \right]}}_{\mathbf{a}_2} = \underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 1 \\ 7\end{array} \right]}}_{\mathbf{a}_3}.
$$

This is equivalent to a system with the augmented matrix
$$
\left[
	{\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & - 1 & - 1 \\ - 2 & 3 & 7\end{array}}
	\right].
$$

If we reduced this matrix to the *reduced* row echelon form, we get

$$
\left[
	{\begin{array}{cc|c}\bbox[3pt,lightgray]{ {\color{blue}1}} & 0 & {\color{red}4} \\ 0 & \bbox[3pt,lightgray]{ {\color{blue}1}} & {\color{red}5}\end{array}}
	\right].
$$

Finally, the third column of the *reduced* matrix tells us that $x_1=4$ and $x_2=5,$ meaning that
$$
\underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 1 \\ 7\end{array} \right]}}_{\mathbf{a}_3} = {\color{red}4}\cdot \underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ - 2\end{array} \right]}}_{\mathbf{a}_1} + {\color{red}5}\cdot \underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 1 \\ 3\end{array} \right]}}_{\mathbf{a}_2}.
$$

**Watch out!** The matrix must be written in *reduced* row echelon form (with $1$'s for pivots and $0$'s above and below the pivots), not just row echelon form.

Note that the number of pivot columns always coincides with the number of non-zero rows in the corresponding row echelon form matrix.
So, technically, 

$\textrm{rank}(A)$ is the number of *pivot columns* in the corresponding row echelon form matrix of $A$.

Or, equivalently,

$\textrm{rank}(A)$ is the number of *non-zero rows* in the corresponding row echelon form matrix of $A$.

We say that two vectors $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ are **linearly independent** if the only solution to the equation

$$
x_1 \mathbf{v}_1 + x_2 \mathbf{v}_2 = \mathbf{0}
$$

is $x_1 = x_2 = 0.$ Otherwise, if there exists any solution other than $x_1 = x_2 = 0,$ then we say that the two vectors $\mathbf{v}_1$ and $\mathbf{v}_2$ are **linearly dependent**.

To illustrate, let's consider two sets of vectors in $\mathbb{R}^2\mathbin{:}$

$$
{\color{blue}
\textrm{I.}\:\: \Bigg\{ \underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 0\end{array} \right]}}_{\mathbf{a}_1}, \underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}0 \\ 1\end{array} \right]}}_{\mathbf{a}_2} \Bigg\}
}
{\color{red}
\qquad\qquad
\textrm{II.}\:\: \Bigg\{ \underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 1\end{array} \right]}}_{\mathbf{b}_1}, \underbrace{ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 2 \\ - 2\end{array} \right]}}_{\mathbf{b}_2} \Bigg\}
}
$$

- For the first set ${\color{blue}(\textrm{I})},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{a}_{1}+{x}_{2}{a}_{2} & =0 \\ {x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1\end{bmatrix} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation is true only if $x_1=x_2=0.$ So, the set $\color{blue}(\textrm{I})$ is *linearly independent*.

- On the other hand, for the second set ${\color{red}(\textrm{II})},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2} & =0 \\ {x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The above equation has solutions other than $x_1=x_2=0.$ For example, $x_1=2$ and $x_2=1$ gives
$$
2 \cdot {\color{red}{\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 1\end{array} \right]}} + 1 \cdot {\color{red}{\left[ \begin{array}{c}- 2 \\ - 2\end{array} \right]}} = \mathbf{0}.
$$
Therefore, the set $\color{red}(\textrm{II})$ is *not* linearly independent. Rather, it is *linearly dependent*.

**Note:** You may notice that the vectors in the set $\color{red}(\textrm{II})$ were parallel (i.e. multiples of one another), while the vectors in set $\color{blue}(\textrm{I})$ were not. This trend holds in general, for all sets of two vectors:

- a set of two vectors is *linearly dependent* if and only if the two vectors are parallel, while

- a set of two vectors is *linearly independent* if and only if the two vectors are not parallel.

Any set of two vectors that contains the zero vector $\mathbf{0}$ must be linearly dependent. To see this, consider the set $\left\{ \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{0} \right\}.$ We can realize that this set is linearly dependent using either of the following two methods.

**Method 1**

Notice that 

$$
0 \cdot \mathbf{v} + 1 \cdot \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}.
$$

Therefore, the equation

$$
x_1 \mathbf{v} + x_2 \cdot \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}
$$

has a solution $x_1=0$ and $x_2=1,$ which is different from $x_1=x_2=0.$ So, the set is linearly dependent.

**Method 2**

Alternatively, recall that a set of two vectors is linearly dependent if and only if the two vectors are parallel. That is, the two vectors are multiples of each other.

The zero vector $\mathbf{0}$ is parallel to every other vector because it is a multiple of any other vector. For any vector $\mathbf{v},$ we have

$$
\mathbf{0} = 0 \cdot \mathbf{v} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \mathbf{0} \parallel \mathbf{v}.
$$

So, because $\mathbf{0}$ is parallel to $\mathbf{v},$ the set $\left\{ \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{0} \right\}$ is linearly dependent.

So far, we've discussed linear dependence and linear independence for sets of two vectors. However, these concepts can be extended to sets of any number of vectors.

A set of $n$ vectors $\left\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_n \right\}$ is called **linearly independent** if the only solution to the equation

$$
x_1 \mathbf{v}_1 + x_2 \mathbf{v}_2 + \ldots + x_n \mathbf{v}_n = \mathbf{0}
$$

is $x_1=x_2=\ldots=x_n=0.$ Otherwise, if there exists any solution other than $x_1 = x_2 = \ldots = x_n = 0,$ then we say that the set $\left\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_n \right\}$ is **linearly dependent**.

Similar to sets containing two vectors, a general set of $n$ vectors is dependent if *any* two vectors in the set are parallel.

**But be careful!** When working with sets containing more than two vectors, having a linearly dependent set is possible even if *none* of the vectors are parallel! 

For example, consider the following set of vectors: 

$$
\left\{
	{\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 0\end{array} \right]},
	{\left[ \begin{array}{c}0 \\ 1\end{array} \right]},
	{\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 1\end{array} \right]}
	\right\}
$$

None of the vectors in this set are parallel. However, we have

$$
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 0\end{array} \right]} + {\left[ \begin{array}{c}0 \\ 1\end{array} \right]} - {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 1\end{array} \right]} = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}0 \\ 0\end{array} \right]}.
$$

So, the equation

$$
x_1 \cdot {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 0\end{array} \right]} + x_2 \cdot {\left[ \begin{array}{c}0 \\ 1\end{array} \right]}+ x_3 \cdot {\left[ \begin{array}{c}1 \\ 1\end{array} \right]} = {\left[ \begin{array}{c}0 \\ 0\end{array} \right]}
$$

has a solution $x_1 = 1,$ $x_2 = 1,$ and $x_3 = -1,$ which is different from $x_1 = x_2 = x_3 = 0.$ Therefore, we conclude that the vectors are linearly dependent.

As with sets containing only two vectors, any set of vectors that contains the zero vector $\mathbf{0}$ must be linearly dependent. 

To see this, consider the set 

$$
\left\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_{n-1}, \mathbf{0} \right\}.
$$

 

Notice that 

$$
0 \cdot \mathbf{v}_1 + 0 \cdot \mathbf{v}_2 + \ldots + 0 \cdot \mathbf{v}_{n-1} + 1 \cdot \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}.
$$

So, the equation

$$
x_1 \mathbf{v}_1 + x_2 \mathbf{v}_2 + \ldots + x_{n-1} \mathbf{v}_{n-1} + x_n \cdot \mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0}
$$

has the solution $x_1=x_2=\ldots = x_{n-1}=0$ and $x_n=1,$ which is different from $x_1=x_2=\ldots = x_n=0.$ Therefore, the set is linearly dependent.

The set of vectors $\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{v}_n \}$ in an abstract vector space $V$ is **linearly dependent** if there exist real scalars $x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n$ not all zero such that 

$$
x_1\mathbf{v}_1+x_2\mathbf{v}_2+\ldots+x_n\mathbf{v}_n=\mathbf{0}.
$$

Otherwise, if $x_1 = x_2 = \cdots = x_n = 0$ is the only solution, the set is **linearly independent**.

Let's consider some examples.

- First, let's consider the vector space $\mathbb{R}[t]$ of all polynomials in variable $t,$ along with the set

$$
S = \big\{ \underbrace{1}_{\color{blue}p_1(t)}, \: \underbrace{t}_{\color{blue}p_2(t)}, \: \underbrace{t^2}_{\color{blue}p_3(t)} \big\}.
$$

To determine whether $S$ is linearly dependent in $\mathbb{R}[t],$ we must solve the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t)+{x}_{3}{p}_{3}(t) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the given expressions for $p_1(t),p_2(t)$ and $p_3(t)$ into the above equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\cdot 1+{x}_{2}\cdot t+{x}_{3}\cdot {t}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}t+{x}_{3}{t}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation is true for every $t$ if and only if 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} &=0 \\ {x}_{2} &=0 \\ {x}_{3} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Since $x_1 = x_2 = x_3 = 0$ is the only solution, $S$ is linearly independent in $\mathbb R[t].$

- Let's consider the vector space $\mathbb R[t]$ once more, along with the set 

$$
T = \big\{ \underbrace{t^2+1}_{\color{red}q_1(t)}, \: \underbrace{-2t^2-2}_{\color{red}q_2(t)} \big\}.
$$

To determine whether $T$ is linearly dependent in $\mathbb{R}[t],$ we must solve the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{q}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{q}_{2}(t) & =0 \\ {x}_{1}({t}^{2}+1)+{x}_{2}(-2{t}^{2}-2) & =0 \\ ({x}_{1}-2{x}_{2})+({x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}){t}^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation is true for every $t$ if and only if 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} &=0 \\ {x}_{1}-2{x}_{2} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

This system has the nonzero solution $(x_1,x_2)=(2,1).$ As a result, we get

$$
2 \cdot {\color{red}q_1(t)} + 1 \cdot {\color{red}q_2(t)} = 0.
$$

Therefore, the set $\big\{ q_1(t), q_2(t) \big\}$ is linearly dependent in $\mathbb R[t].$

Note the following important property of linearly dependent sets.

*A set of vectors is linearly dependent if and only if it contains a vector that is a linear combination of **other** vectors from that set.*

To see why this is true, let $\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2,\cdots, \mathbf{v}_n\}$ be a linearly dependent set of $n$ vectors. This means that the equation

$$
x_1\mathbf{v}_1 + x_2 \mathbf{v}_2 + \cdots + x_n\mathbf{v}_n = \mathbf{0}
$$

has a non-trivial solution, i.e. a solution in which at least one of the coefficients $x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n$ is not zero. Without loss of generality, we may assume that $x_1 \ne 0,$ and we can rewrite the above equation as

$$
\mathbf{v}_1 = -\dfrac{x_2}{x_1} \mathbf{v}_2 - \dfrac{x_3}{x_1}\mathbf{v}_3 - \cdots - \dfrac{x_n}{x_1}\mathbf{v}_n.
$$

The above argument shows that the vector $\mathbf{v}_1$ can be written as a linear combination of the other vectors from the set.

A set of vectors 

$$
\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_n \}
$$

is called a **basis** of an abstract vector space $V$ if the following two conditions hold:

- $\mathcal{B}$ is linearly independent, and

- $\mathcal{B}$ spans $V.$

For example, let's consider the vector space $\mathbb{R}_2[t]$ of all polynomials in the variable $t$ over $\mathbb R$ with degree at most $2,$ and its subset 

$$
\mathcal{B} = \left\{ {\color{blue}{1}}, {\color{blue}{t}}, {\color{blue}{t^2}} \right\}.
$$

 

Is $\mathcal{B}$ a basis for $\mathbb{R}_2[t]?$ Let's check our two conditions.

- First, we check for linear independence. Notice that the equation 

$$
x_1 \cdot {\color{blue}1} + x_2 \cdot {\color{blue}t} + x_3 \cdot {\color{blue}t^2} = 0
$$

 
is true for all $t$ if and only if 

$$
x_1=x_2=x_3=0.
$$

Therefore, the set $\mathcal{B}$ is linearly independent in $\mathbb{R}_2[t].$

- Next, we check that $\mathcal B$ spans $\mathbb{R}_2[t].$ Notice that we can write any polynomial $at^2+bt+c\in\mathbb{R}_2[t]$ as a linear combination of vectors from $\mathcal{B} \mathbin{:}$

$$
at^2+bt+c=c\cdot{\color{blue}1} + b\cdot{\color{blue}t} + a\cdot{\color{blue}t^2}
$$

Therefore, $\mathcal B$ spans $\mathbb{R}_2[t].$

Since both conditions hold, we conclude that $\mathcal{B} = \{ {1}, {t}, {t^2} \}$ is a basis of $\mathbb{R}_2[t]$.

A set of vectors $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_n \}$ is a basis of a vector space $V$ if $\mathcal{B}$ is a **maximally linearly independent set in $V$**. In other words, $\mathcal{B}$ is linearly independent and for any vector ${\color{blue}\mathbf{w}} \in V,$ the set 

$$
\mathcal{B} \cup \{ {\color{blue}\mathbf{w}} \} = \{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2, \ldots, \mathbf{b}_n, {\color{blue}\mathbf{w}} \}
$$

is linearly dependent.

Let $\mathbb{R}_n[t]$ denote the vector space of all polynomials in the variable $t$ over $\mathbb{R}$ that have degree at most $n.$ Also, let $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ be the vector space of all $2 \times 2$ matrices over $\mathbb{R}.$ Then, we have the following important standard bases.

- The standard basis of $\mathbb{R}_1[t]$ is $\{ 1, \: t \}.$

- The standard basis of $\mathbb{R}_2[t]$ is $\{ 1, \: t, \: t^2 \}.$

- The standard basis of $\mathbb{R}_n[t]$ is $\{ 1, \: t, \: \ldots, \: t^n \}.$

- The standard basis of $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ is
$$
\left\{ {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{array} \right]}, {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{array} \right]}, {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{array} \right]}, {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{array} \right]} \right\}.
$$

Applying a row operation to any $3\times 3$ matrix is the same as *pre-multiplying* (multiplying on the left) the matrix by the corresponding elementary matrix.

For instance, if we wish to swap the first row and the second row of a $3\times 3$ matrix $A,$ we pre-multiply $A$ by the corresponding elementary matrix 
$$
E_1 = {\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array} \right]} 
	\qquad
	(R_1\leftrightarrow R_2)
$$
to get $E_1 A.$

To perform a sequence of row operations to a $3\times 3$ matrix, we pre-multiply the matrix by the elementary matrix corresponding to the first operation, and then pre-multiply the result by the elementary matrix corresponding to the second operation.

For instance, given a $3 \times 3$ matrix $A,$ suppose that we would like to multiply the second row by $2$ and then add $3$ times the first row to the second row. To do this, we first pre-multiply $A$ by 
$$
E_2 = {\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array} \right]} 
	\qquad
	(R_2 := 2R_2).
$$
to get $E_2 A.$ Then we pre-multiply the result by 
$$
E_3 = {\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{array} \right]} 
	\qquad
	(R_2 := R_2 + 3R_1)
$$ 
to get $E_3 E_2 A.$

If an $n\!\times \!n$ matrix $A$ has an entire row or column of zeros, then its determinant is equal to zero.

For example, consider the matrix $A$ given below:

$$
A=
{\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}∗ & ∗ & ∗ \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ ∗ & ∗ & ∗\end{array} \right]}
$$

The second row consists of all zeros, and the asterisks ($\ast$) may represent any number.

Let's compute the determinant using the Laplace expansion across the second row:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}∗ & ∗ & ∗ \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ ∗ & ∗ & ∗\end{vmatrix} \\  & =(-1)^{2+1}(0)\begin{vmatrix}∗ & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗\end{vmatrix}+(-1)^{2+2}(0)\begin{vmatrix}∗ & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗\end{vmatrix}+(-1)^{2+3}(0)\begin{vmatrix}∗ & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗\end{vmatrix} \\  & =0+0+0 \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that it doesn't matter what numbers are represented by the asterisks ($\ast$). Each cofactor is multiplied by zero, so the final result must be zero.

Now, suppose a matrix has no zero rows but it has two identical rows:

$$
A  = {\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}{\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}1} \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ {\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}1}\end{array} \right]}.
$$

We can subtract the $1$st row from the $3$rd row, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 1 & 2 & 1\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =B\end{aligned}
$$

Since this operation does not change the determinant, we get $\det(A) = \det(B).$ Furthermore, as $B$ contains a zero row, we obtain

$$
\det(A) = \det(B) = 0.
$$

Notice that we can use this method with columns too. Therefore, we have the following property:

*If a square matrix has at least two identical rows/columns, its determinant equals zero.*

Now, suppose a matrix has no zero rows and no identical rows but it has two proportional rows:

$$
A  = {\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}{\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}2} & {\color{blue}1} \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ {\color{blue}- 3} & {\color{blue}- 6} & {\color{blue}- 3}\end{array} \right]}
$$

We can add three times the $1$st row to the $3$rd row, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ -3 & -6 & -3\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =B\end{aligned}
$$

Since this operation does not change the determinant, we get $\det(A) = \det(B).$ Furthermore, as $B$ contains a zero row, we obtain

$$
\det(A) = \det(B) = 0.
$$

Notice that we can use this method with columns too. Therefore, we have the following property:

*If a square matrix has at least two proportional rows/columns, its determinant equals zero.*

In conclusion, if an $n\!\times \!n$ matrix $A$ satisfies any one of the following conditions, then $\det(A)=0.$

I. $A$ has a zero row/column

II. $A$ has two identical rows/columns

III. $A$ has two proportional rows/columns

IV. $A$ has a row/column that is a linear combination of other rows/columns

Notice that condition IV encompasses each of the conditions I, II, and III. If we have a zero row/column, two identical rows/columns, or proportional rows/columns, then the rows/columns form a linearly dependent set of vectors. 
In turn, this means that one of the rows/columns is a linear combination of other rows/columns.

**Watch out!** While all of the above conditions are *sufficient* to conclude that $\det(A)=0,$ only condition IV is *necessary* to conclude that $\det(A)=0.$ 
In other words, if we have a matrix $A$ with $\det(A)=0,$ then conditions I, II, and III may or may not be satisfied, while condition IV *must* be satisfied. 

So, we have the following theorem:

*$\det(A)=0$ if and only if one of the rows/columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other rows/columns of $A.$*

Finally, note also that in the case of a $2\times 2$ matrix *only*, statements III and IV mean the same thing.

Geometrically, the absolute value of an $n \times n$ determinant can be interpreted as the volume of the $n$-dimensional parallelepiped spanned by the columns of the determinant. 

For example:

- Suppose the columns of a $3\times 3$ matrix $A$ are ${\color{black}\mathbf{a}}, {\color{black}\mathbf{b}},$ and ${\color{black}\mathbf{c}}.$
$$
A = {\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}{\color{black}|} & {\color{black}|} & {\color{black}|} \\ {\color{black}\mathbf{a}} & {\color{black}\mathbf{b}} & {\color{black}\mathbf{c}} \\ {\color{black}|} & {\color{black}|} & {\color{black}|}\end{array} \right]}
$$
The $3$-dimensional parallelepiped spanned by the columns of $A$ is depicted below:

![](images/25/2597b48a010607fca71c551dbce8e9e2bbeda47d0892a582347ae1cdf19f1bf6.png)

The volume $V$ of this parallelepiped equals the absolute value of the determinant of $A{:}$

$$
V = \left|\det(A)\right|
$$

- Now suppose the columns of a $2\times 2$ matrix $B$ are ${\color{black}\mathbf{p}}$ and ${\color{black}\mathbf{q}}.$
$$
B = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}{\color{black}|} & {\color{black}|} \\ {\color{black}\mathbf{p}} & {\color{black}\mathbf{q}} \\ {\color{black}|} & {\color{black}|}\end{array} \right]}
$$
The $2$-dimensional parallelepiped (i.e., the parallelogram) spanned by vectors $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ is shown below:

![](images/4a/4af1971404b188df75bb3d62d47ac95340c5e1791066e5358370d743230baa45.png)

The two-dimensional volume $V$ (i.e., the area) of this parallelepiped equals the absolute value of the determinant of $B{:}$

$$
V = \left|\det(B)\right|
$$

- In general, the absolute value of the determinant of an $n\times n$ matrix $M$ gives the $n$-dimensional volume of the parallelepiped spanned by the columns of $M.$

In this lesson, we studied the following property:

*$\det(A) = 0$ if and only if one of the columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other columns of $A$.*

What does this property mean in geometric terms?

The component $\det(A) = 0$ implies that the $n$-dimensional parallelepiped formed by the columns of $A$ has zero volume. Conversely, when one of the columns of $A$ is a linear combination of other columns, it indicates that the corresponding parallelepiped possesses at most $n-1$ distinct dimensions. 

Consider the following examples:

- In the case of a $3$-dimensional parallelepiped, if the vector $\mathbf{c}$ is a linear combination of the vectors $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$, then $\mathbf{c}$ lies within the plane containing $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$. In other words, the vectors $\mathbf{a}$, $\mathbf{b}$, and $\mathbf{c}$ are coplanar. Consequently, we obtain a "flat" ($2$-dimensional) figure with a volume of $0$.

- For the parallelogram example, if the vector $\mathbf{q}$ is a linear combination of the vector $\mathbf{p}$ (i.e., $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ are proportional), then $\mathbf{q}$ resides on the line containing vector $\mathbf{p}$. In other words, the vectors $\mathbf{p}$ and $\mathbf{q}$ are collinear. This results in a $1$-dimensional object with a $2$-dimensional volume (i.e., area) of $0$.

Consider the system of linear equations



$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+z &=1 \\ y+z &=-2 \\ -x+2y+z &=-1.\end{aligned}\right.
$$



Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 2 & 1 & -1\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 0\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+z &=1 \\ y+z &=-2 \\ z &=2,\end{aligned}\right.
$$



and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=2$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y+(2) &=-2\,⟹\,y=-4.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=-4$ and $z=2$ into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-(-4)+(2) &=1\,⟹\,x=-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-5,$ $y=-4,$ and $z=2.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle -5,-4,2 \rangle.$

Consider the system of linear equations


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=-2 \\ x+y+2z &=-1 \\ x+2y+z &=1.\end{aligned}\right.
$$



Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.

The augmented matrix for this system is



$$
M= \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right].
$$



Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 1 & 1 & 2 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get $a_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+z &=-2 \\ y &=3 \\ z &=1,\end{aligned}\right.
$$



and we can apply back substitution. The third equation $z=1$ tells us the value of $z,$ and the second equation $y=3$ tells us the value of $y.$ Substituting these values into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x+(3)+(1) &=-2\,⟹\,x=-6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=-6,$ $y=3,$ and $z=1.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle -6,3,1 \rangle.$

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 25\end{array}\right].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 1 & 3 & 2 & 25\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 6\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}-2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 0 & -4 & -20\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :=-\frac{1}{4}{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 1 & 2 & 19 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 & 13 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y+2z &=19 \\ y+2z &=13 \\ z &=5,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The final equation $z=5$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
y+2(5)=13\,⟹\,y=13-10=3.
$$

Finally, substituting both $y=3$ and $z=5$ into the first equation, we get

$$
x+(3)+2(5)=19\,⟹\,x=6.
$$

Therefore, the solution is $x=6,y=3$, and $z=5.$ Or, in vector form, $⟨6,3,5⟩.$

Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+2z &=8 \\ -2x+2y-3z &=-11 \\ x+z &=9.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then solve the linear system.

The augmented matrix for this system is

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ -2 & 2 & -3 & -11 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 9\end{array}\right].
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ -2 & 2 & -3 & -11 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 9\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 & 9\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 1\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we get ${a}_{22}=0.$ Therefore, we swap the $2$nd and $3$rd rows:

$$
\begin{aligned} & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 & 1\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & ↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 2 & 8 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 5\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

So, the system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y+2z &=8 \\ y-z &=1 \\ z &=5,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

and we can apply back substitution. The third equation $z=5$ tells us the value of $z.$ Substituting this value into the second equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(5) &=1\,⟹\,y=6.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, substituting $y=6$ and $z=5$ into the first equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}x-(6)+2(5) &=8\,⟹\,x=4.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, the solution is $x=4$, $y=6$, and $z=5.$

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 


$$
M= \left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -3 & 1 \\ 4 & -12 & 4\end{array}\right].
$$



Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form, and then find the general solution of the linear system represented by the matrix.

Reducing $M$ to echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -3 & 1 \\ 4 & -12 & 4\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now



$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-3y &=1 \\ 0x+0y &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$



Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y = 0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x - 3y = 1.
$$

The first variable $(x)$ is the basic variable, and the second variable $(y)$ is the free variable. Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x=1+3y,$ and the general solution is



$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=1+3y \\ y &=y\end{aligned}\right.
$$



where $y$ is an arbitrary number. 

In vector form, the general solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1+3y \\ y\end{bmatrix}=⟨1+3y,\,y⟩,\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear equations


$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then find the general solution of the linear system.

First, we set up the augmented matrix for the system:



$$
M = \left[\begin{array}{cc|c}2 & 5 & 4 \\ 4 & 10 & 0\end{array}\right]
$$



Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}2 & 5 & 4 \\ 4 & 10 & 0\end{array}\right] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & \frac{5}{2} & 2 \\ 4 & 10 & 0\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & \frac{5}{2} & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -8\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now


$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+\frac{5}{2}y &=2 \\ 0x+0y &=-8.\end{aligned}\right.

However, the final equation $0x+0y=-8$ has no solution. It simplifies to $0=-8,$ which is a false statement.

$$

is $x_1 = x_2 = 0.$ Otherwise, the vectors are *linearly dependent*.

A set containing *only two* vectors is linearly *dependent* if and only if the two vectors are parallel.

{x}_{1}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}}_{{a}_{1}}+{x}_{2}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3 \\ -5\end{bmatrix}}_{{a}_{2}}+{x}_{3}\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}}_{{a}_{3}}=\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}}_{{a}_{4}}.
$$

This equation is equivalent to the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=-1 \\ -2{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3} &=2 \\ 5{x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}+6{x}_{3} &=2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

$$
\begin{aligned} & \,\,\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & -1 \\ -2 & 3 & -2 & 2 \\ 5 & -5 & 6 & 2\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & -5 & 6 & 2\end{array}\right] & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-5){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{array}\right] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+(-1){R}_{3} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -1 & 0 & -8 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{array}\right] & {R}_{1} & :={R}_{1}+{R}_{2} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 0 & 0 & -8 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

From the reduced matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st, $2$nd, and $3$rd columns. So,  $B$ is indeed a basis of $\text{Span}\{{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3},{a}_{4}\}.$
Also, the matrix tells us that ${x}_{1}=-8,$ ${x}_{2}=0,$ and ${x}_{3}=7,$ meaning that

$$
(-8)\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}}_{{a}_{1}}+0\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 3 \\ -5\end{bmatrix}}_{{a}_{2}}+7\cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -2 \\ 6\end{bmatrix}}_{{a}_{3}}=\underbrace{\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}}_{{a}_{4}}.
$$

Therefore, ${x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=-8+0+7=-1.$

Consider a vector space $V$ and vectors $\mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3 \in V.$ Given that $\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3\}$ is linearly independent, which of the following statements are true?

- $\{ 4\mathbf{v}_1, 5\mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3\}$ is linearly independent

- $\{ \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{v}_1, 2\mathbf{v}_2 \}$ is linearly independent

- $\{ \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3 \}$ is linearly independent

Let's examine each of the given options in turn.

- Statement I is true. Suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(4{v}_{1})+{x}_{2}(5{v}_{2})+{x}_{3}{v}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, in turn, gives

$$
\begin{aligned}(4{x}_{1}){v}_{1}+(5{x}_{2}){v}_{2}+{x}_{3}{v}_{3} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3\}$ is a linearly independent set, the final equation can be true only if

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}4{x}_{1} &=0 \\ 5{x}_{2} &=0 \\ {x}_{3} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The unique solution of the system is $x_1=x_2=x_3=0,$ which means that 

$$
\{ 4\mathbf{v}_1, 5\mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3\}
$$

 is linearly independent.

- Statement II is false. Indeed, notice that

$$
1 \cdot \mathbf{0} + 0 \cdot \mathbf{v}_1 + 0 \cdot (2\mathbf{v}_2) = \mathbf{0}.
$$

As a result, $x_1\mathbf{0}+x_2\mathbf{v}_1+x_3(2\mathbf{v}_2)=\mathbf{0}$ has a non-zero solution. This means that $\{ \mathbf{0}, \mathbf{v}_1, 2\mathbf{v}_2 \}$ is linearly dependent. In general, any set containing the zero vector is linearly dependent.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, $x_1\mathbf{v}_2+x_2\mathbf{v}_3=\mathbf{0}$ must have only the zero solution $x_1=x_2=0.$  If this equation has a non-zero solution, $a \cdot \mathbf{v}_2 + b \cdot \mathbf{v}_3=\mathbf{0},$ then we obtain

$$
0 \cdot \mathbf{v}_1 + a \cdot \mathbf{v}_2 + b \cdot \mathbf{v}_3 = \mathbf{0},
$$

which would mean that $\{ \mathbf{v}_1, \mathbf{v}_2, \mathbf{v}_3\}$ is linearly dependent.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

Consider the set of matrices $\big\{A, B \big\},$ where 
$$
A= {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}1 & 0 \\ - 2 & 4\end{array} \right]}, 
	\qquad
	B= {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}3 & 5 \\ 2 & - 6\end{array} \right]}.
$$
If the set is linearly dependent, find the value of $\dfrac{x_1}{x_2}$ from a non-zero solution of $x_1A+x_2B=O,$ where $O$ is the $2 \times 2$ zero-matrix.

If the set is linearly dependent, then there exist $x_1,x_2$ not both zero such that 

$$
x_1A+x_2B=O.
$$

Otherwise, if $x_1 = x_2 = 0,$ the set is linearly independent.

Substituting the matrices $A$ and $B$ into the above equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -2 & 4\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}3 & 5 \\ 2 & -6\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} & 0 \\ -2{x}_{1} & 4{x}_{1}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3{x}_{2} & 5{x}_{2} \\ 2{x}_{2} & -6{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\ \begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} & 5{x}_{2} \\ -2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} & 4{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Equating the corresponding entries, we obtain the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} &=0 \\ 5{x}_{2} &=0 \\ -2{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2} &=0 \\ 4{x}_{1}-6{x}_{2} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we consider the corresponding augmented matrix and reduce it to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ -2 & 2 & 0 \\ 4 & -6 & 0\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+2{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+(-4){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 8 & 0 \\ 0 & -18 & 0\end{array}\right] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+\left(-\frac{8}{5}\right){R}_{2} \\ {R}_{4}:={R}_{4}+\frac{18}{5}{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right]\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. Therefore, we get the system

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2} &=0 \\ 5{x}_{2} &=0,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

which has only the zero solution $x_1=x_2=0.$

Consequently, $\big\{A, B \big\}$ is linearly independent.

Consider the set $\big\{ p_1(t), p_2(t),p_3(t) \big\}$ of polynomials from $\mathbb{R}[t],$ where

$$
p_1(t)=1+t, \qquad 
p_2(t)=-2t-4, \qquad
p_3(t)=-2t-3.
$$

If the set is linearly dependent, find the value of $\dfrac{x_2}{x_1}$ from a non-zero solution of $x_1 \cdot p_1(t)+x_2 \cdot p_2(t) + x_3 \cdot p_3(t)=0.$

If the set is linearly dependent, then there exist $x_1,x_2,x_3$ not all zero such that 

$$
x_1p_1(t)+x_2p_2(t)+x_3p_3(t)=0.
$$

Otherwise, if $x_1 = x_2 = x_3 = 0,$ the set is linearly independent.

Substituting the given expressions for $p_1(t),p_2(t),$ and $p_3(t)$ into the above equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(1+t)+{x}_{2}(-2t-4)+{x}_{3}(-2t-3) & =0 \\ ({x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3})+({x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3})t & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The final equation is true for every $t$ if and only if 

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3} &=0 \\ {x}_{1}-2{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Now, we consider the corresponding augmented matrix and reduce it to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -4 & -3 & 0 \\ 1 & -2 & -2 & 0\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & -4 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 2 & 1 & 0\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd. Hence, $x_3$ is a free variable. The system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}-3{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 2{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

From the second equation, we get $x_2=-\dfrac 12x_3.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get

$$
x_1-4\left(-\dfrac 12x_3\right)-3x_3=0 \qquad\Longrightarrow \qquad x_1=x_3.
$$

Therefore, the general solution is
$$
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{array} \right]}
	=
	{\left[ \begin{array}{c}{x}_{3} \\ - {\displaystyle \frac{1}{2}} {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{array} \right]},\qquad x_3 \in \mathbb{R}.
$$
Finally, for any $x_3 \neq 0,$ we obtain 

$$
\dfrac{x_2}{x_1}=\dfrac{\left( -\dfrac 12x_3\right)}{x_3}=-\dfrac 12.
$$

Consider the vector space $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$ of all $2 \times 2$ matrices over $\mathbb{R}.$

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $$
\displaystyle \bigg\{ {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & - 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{array} \right]}, {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{array} \right]} \bigg\}
$$ is a linearly independent set in $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$

II. $\begin{bmatrix}0 & -2 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $$
\displaystyle \bigg\{ {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & - 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{array} \right]}, {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{array} \right]} \bigg\}
$$

III. $$
\displaystyle \bigg\{ {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & - 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{array} \right]}, {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{array} \right]} \bigg\}
$$ is a basis of $\text{M}_2(\mathbb{R})$

Let's examine each of the statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation
$$
x_1 \cdot {\color{blue}{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & - 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{array} \right]}} + x_2 \cdot  {\color{blue}{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{array} \right]}} = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{array} \right]}
$$
is true if and only if $x_1=x_2=0.$ So, the set is linearly independent.

- Statement II is true. Indeed,
$$
{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & - 2 \\ 0 & 4\end{array} \right]} = 2 \cdot {\color{blue}{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & - 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{array} \right]}} + 2 \cdot {\color{blue}{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{array} \right]}}.
$$

- Statement III is false. For example, the matrix $\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 5\end{bmatrix}$ can't be written as a linear combination of 
$$
\bigg\{ {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & - 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{array} \right]}, {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{array} \right]} \bigg\}
$$
since all these linear combinations result in matrices with the entry $a_{11} = 0\mathbin{:}$
$$
a \cdot {\color{blue}{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & - 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{array} \right]}} + b \cdot {\color{blue}{\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{array} \right]}} = {\left[ \begin{array}{cc}0 & - a \\ 0 & 2 b\end{array} \right]}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

Let $\mathcal{B}= \left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ be a basis of a vector space $V.$ 

Which of the following statements are true?

I. $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2},- \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_3}+\mathbf{b_1} \right\}$ is a basis of $V$

II. $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{0}  \right\}$ spans $V$

III. $\left\{  -\mathbf{b_2}, 3\mathbf{b_1}\right\}$ is linearly dependent

Since $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis, the following properties must hold:

- $\mathcal{B}$ is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors in $V,$ and

- $\mathcal{B}$ spans $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{2}+{x}_{2}(-{b}_{1})+{x}_{3}({b}_{3}+{b}_{1}) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{b}_{2}+({x}_{3}-{x}_{2}){b}_{1}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since $\left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ is linearly independent, gives
$$
{\left\{  \begin{array}{l}{x}_{1} = 0 \\ {x}_{3} - {x}_{2} = 0 \\ {x}_{3} = 0\end{array} \right. }
	\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
	{\left\{  \begin{array}{l}{x}_{1} = 0 \\ {x}_{2} = 0 \\ {x}_{3} = 0.\end{array} \right. }
$$
Also, $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2},- \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_3}+\mathbf{b_1} \right\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $\mathcal{B}$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2},- \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_3}+\mathbf{b_1} \right\}\mathbin{:}$

$$
x_1\mathbf{b}_1+x_2\mathbf{b}_2+x_3\mathbf{b}_3
=
x_2\mathbf{b}_2+(x_3-x_1)(-\mathbf{b}_1)+x_3 (\mathbf{b_3}+\mathbf{b_1})
$$

- Statement II is false. In order for $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{0}  \right\}$ to span $V,$ every element of $\mathcal{B}$ must be able to be expressed as a linear combination of elements of $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{0}  \right\}.$ But the vector $\mathbf{b}_1 \in \mathcal{B}$ can't be written as a linear combination of the elements of $\left\{ \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3}, \mathbf{0}  \right\}.$

- Statement III is false. If $\left\{  -\mathbf{b_2}, 3\mathbf{b_1}\right\}$ is linearly dependent then there exist $x_1$ and $x_2$ not both zero such that

$$
x_1(-\mathbf{b_2}) + x_2(3\mathbf{b_1}) = \mathbf{0}.
$$

Then, we would have

$$
(3x_2) \cdot \mathbf{b_1} + (-x_1) \cdot \mathbf{b_2} + 0 \cdot \mathbf{b}_3= \mathbf{0}.
$$

But this would mean that $\mathcal{B} = \left\{ \mathbf{b_1}, \mathbf{b_2}, \mathbf{b_3} \right\}$ is linearly dependent, which contradicts the fact that $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis of $V.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

Consider a vector space $V$ and vectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3},{v}_{4}\in V.$ Given that ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$ is linearly independent and ${v}_{4}=3{v}_{1}-2{v}_{2}+5{v}_{3},$ which of the following statements are true?

Consider the set ${{p}_{1}(t),{p}_{2}(t)}$ of polynomials from $R[t],$ where

If the set is linearly dependent, find the value of $\frac{{x}_{2}}{{x}_{1}}$ from a non-zero solution of ${x}_{1}\cdot {p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}\cdot {p}_{2}(t)=0.$

$$
{x}_{1}{p}_{1}(t)+{x}_{2}{p}_{2}(t)=0.

$$

Consider a vector space $V$ and vectors ${v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\in V.$ Given that ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$ is linearly independent, which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

Let's examine each of the given options in turn.

- Statement “${{v}_{1}+{v}_{2},{v}_{2}+{v}_{3},{v}_{3}}$ is linearly independent” is true. Suppose that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}({v}_{1}+{v}_{2})+{x}_{2}({v}_{2}+{v}_{3})+{x}_{3}{v}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, in turn, gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{v}_{1}+({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}){v}_{2}+({x}_{2}+{x}_{3}){v}_{3} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$ is a linearly independent set, the final equation can be true only if

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} &=0 \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2} &=0 \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The unique solution of the system is ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}={x}_{3}=0,$ which means that 

$$
{{v}_{1}+{v}_{2},{v}_{2}+{v}_{3},{v}_{3}}
$$

 is linearly independent.

- Statement “${0,{v}_{1},2{v}_{2}}$ is linearly independent” is false. Indeed, notice that

$$
1\cdot 0+0\cdot {v}_{1}+0\cdot (2{v}_{2})=0.
$$

As a result, ${x}_{1}0+{x}_{2}{v}_{1}+{x}_{3}(2{v}_{2})=0$ has a non-zero solution. This means that ${0,{v}_{1},2{v}_{2}}$ is linearly dependent. In general, any set containing the zero vector is linearly dependent.

- Statement “${{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}$ is linearly independent” is true. Indeed, ${x}_{1}{v}_{1}+{x}_{2}{v}_{2}=0$ must have only the zero solution ${x}_{1}={x}_{2}=0.$  If this equation has a non-zero solution, $a\cdot {v}_{1}+b\cdot {v}_{2}=0,$ then we obtain

$$
a\cdot {v}_{1}+b\cdot {v}_{2}+0\cdot {v}_{3}=0,
$$

which would mean that ${{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}}$ is linearly dependent.

Therefore, the correct answer is “${{v}_{1}+{v}_{2},{v}_{2}+{v}_{3},{v}_{3}}$ is linearly independent”; “${{v}_{1},{v}_{2}}$ is linearly independent” only.

Let $B=\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ be a basis of a vector space $V.$ 

Which of the following statements are true?

Since $B$ is a basis, the following properties must hold:

- $B$ is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors in $V,$ and

- $B$ spans $V.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, if $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2}\}$ is linearly dependent then there exist ${x}_{1}$ and ${x}_{2}$ such that 

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}=0,
$$

where at least one of $x$'s is not zero. But then 

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+0{b}_{3}=0,
$$

which would mean that $B$ is linearly dependent. This would contradict the fact that $B$ is a basis.

- Statement II is false. Since $B$ is a basis of $V,$ it is a maximally linearly independent set of vectors. This means that if we add any new vector to the set, it becomes linearly dependent.

- Statement III is true. Indeed, the equation

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}(2{b}_{1})+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3} & =0\end{aligned}
$$

is equivalent to

$$
\begin{aligned}(2{x}_{1}){b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3} & =0,\end{aligned}
$$

which, since $\{{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent, gives

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}=0 \\ {x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{3}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, $\{2{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}$ spans $V$ since any linear combination of vectors from $B$ can be expressed as a linear combination of $\{2{b}_{1},{b}_{2},{b}_{3}\}:$

$$
{x}_{1}{b}_{1}+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3}=\frac{{x}_{1}}{2}(2{b}_{1})+{x}_{2}{b}_{2}+{x}_{3}{b}_{3}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 & -2 \\ 2 & -3 & -1\end{bmatrix},\,B=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 1 & 8 & -1 \\ 2 & -3 & -1\end{bmatrix}?
$$

Since $det(A)=det(B)$, the row operation applied to $A$ must be to add or subtract a multiple of one row to another row. In other words, it is of the form 

$$
{R}_{j}:={R}_{j}+(k){R}_{i},\,i\ne j.
$$

By considering the given row operations that are of the above form, we notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 3 & 5 & -2 \\ 2 & -3 & -1\end{vmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{3} \\  & =\begin{vmatrix}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 1 & 8 & -1 \\ 2 & -3 & -1\end{vmatrix} \\  & =det(B).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the required row operation is

$$
{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-1){R}_{3}.
$$

Consider the matrices given below. Given that $X$ and $Y$ are row equivalent matrices and $det(X)=5$, find $det(Y).$

$$
X=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -2 \\ -3 & 2 & 2\end{bmatrix},\,Y=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 & 1 \\ -3 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & -2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Notice that $Y$ can be obtained from $X$ by swapping the $2$nd and the $3$rd rows. 

This changes the sign of the determinant to the opposite one.
Therefore, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}det(Y) & =-det(X) \\  & =-(5) \\  & =-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}3 & 9 & -3 \\ 2 & 6 & -2\end{array}\right].
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form, and then find the general solution of the linear system represented by the matrix.

Reducing $M$ to echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}3 & 9 & -3 \\ 2 & 6 & -2\end{array}\right] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 2 & 6 & -2\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+3y &=-1 \\ 0x+0y &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y=0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x+3y=-1.
$$

The first variable $(x)$ is the basic variable, and the second variable $(y)$ is the free variable. Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x=-3y-1,$ and the general solution is

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=-3y-1 \\ y &=y\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $y$ is an arbitrary number. 

In vector form, the general solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3y-1 \\ y\end{bmatrix},\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y &=-1 \\ -4x+8y &=7.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then find the general solution of the linear system.

First, we set up the augmented matrix for the system:

$$
M=\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -2 & -1 \\ -4 & 8 & 7\end{array}\right]
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -2 & -1 \\ -4 & 8 & 7\end{array}\right] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1 & -2 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{array}\right].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y &=-1 \\ 0x+0y &=3.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

However, the final equation $0x+0y=3$ has no solution. It simplifies to $0=3,$ which is a false statement.

So, there is no pair $x,y$ that satisfies both equations in the system. Consequently, the overall system has no solution.
